transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-06 16:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Meyer (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Ethan Cole (Verdant Head of ML), Maya Ruiz (Verdant Platform Engineer), Oliver Park (Verdant Procurement)

Summary: Quick intros, then deep into unit economics — per-token math, batching/caching impacts, routing to dedicated vs hosted, security/residency constraints, and pilot next steps.

[00:00:00] Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for joining. i'm jordan from redwood, and with me is priya our se. quick round robin?
[00:00:18] Ethan: yeah i'm ethan cole, head of ml at verdant. we've been prototyping a chat summarization feature and trying to get a handle on cost and latency at scale.
[00:00:32] Maya: maya here, platform eng, i'll own infra questions.
[00:00:40] Oliver: oliver, procurement, i'll be watching timelines and doc needs, quick intro.
[00:00:48] Jordan: great. goal for today is to map your cost targets, tradeoffs between hosted/dedicated/private and surface a pilot path. doesn't have to be final, just to align.
[00:01:05] Priya: quick note — we'll ask about typical payload sizes and rate patterns. that drives batching/windowing and kv cache effectiveness.
[00:01:21] Ethan: sure, rough numbers: avg prompt 400 tokens, responses ~600 tokens, 1k-2k requests per minute during peak.
[00:01:34] Maya: and we have spikes up to 5k rpm when marketing events happen.
[00:01:42] Priya: okay that profile is super helpful. two levers we'll call out: batching (how many concurrent requests we can pack per GPU step) and prefix/KV caching for repeated prefixes, both reduce per-token compute.
[00:01:58] Jordan: we should set a target metric — what's acceptable latency P95?
[00:02:06] Ethan: for chat UX, p95 under 1.2s is ideal, 2s acceptable.
[00:02:12] Jordan: noted. hosted can hit that with small-model variants and smart routing; dedicated gives more throughput predictability but requires commit.
[00:02:25] Oliver: pricing question — we're tracking monthly spend caps. is there a clear cutoff where dedicated becomes cheaper than hosted?
[00:02:34] Priya: yes — it's about qps, token mix, and desired tail latency. quick rule of thumb: at steady-state sustained high qps (e.g., several hundred rps for heavy gen) dedicated often wins on $/token after reserved commitments and optimized batching. but hosted gives flexibility without ops.
[00:02:55] Ethan: can you give an example calculation?
[00:03:00] Jordan: sure — here's a simplified run: assume 1M tokens/day produced, model throughput on a shared host might mean $X per 1k tokens; with caching and batching you might reduce effective tokens by 15-30% for our use case. with dedicated and 50% better batching you lower cost further. i'll send the workbook.
[00:03:23] Maya: when you say "tokens reduced" with caching is that dedup or prefix? we have a lot of repeated system prompts.
[00:03:31] Priya: mostly prefix/KV caching — repeated system prompts and instruction templates hit cache so you only pay for the delta generation. also determinism of prompts matters; noisy user messages reduce cache hit.
[00:03:45] Ethan: hmm we do a lot of template-based instructions, so cache should help. what's the effort to enable that?
[00:03:53] Priya: on hosted it's mostly config and ensuring consistent prompt shaping. on private/dedicated we can tune cache size and pin hot keys to GPUs; there's a bit more ops but more control.
[00:04:10] Jordan: also quantization/precision matters — 4-bit vs 8-bit tradeoffs. we can recommend quant profiles that keep quality while reducing flop cost.
[00:04:22] Maya: we care about hallucination and answer quality — any quality regressions with aggressive quant?
[00:04:29] Priya: small chance depending on the model family; we'll pair quant recommendations with an eval suite. that's part of the pilot.
[00:04:38] [00:05:00] Ethan: on security — do you offer KMS and customer-managed keys? we need keys kept in our cloud, not Redwood.
[00:05:08] Jordan: yes, private deployments support customer KMS/HSM; dedicated has integrations too. hosted can integrate with envelope encryption and SOC2 certs, but for full key custody you'd look at private.
[00:05:22] Oliver: and audit logs / SSO?
[00:05:25] Priya: RBAC, SAML SSO, and audit trails are supported across enterprise plans. we'll include the SOC 2 / ISO docs in the folder.
[00:05:36] Ethan: for cost planning, we'd like to see a scenario: hosted at current qps, hosted with 30% cache hit, and dedicated with reserved instance pricing and optimized batching. can you model that?
[00:05:49] Jordan: yes that's exactly what the workbook will show. i'll populate it with your token counts and traffic shape.
[00:05:55] Maya: on latency — if we go dedicated, what's the typical p95 impact after batching?
[00:06:02] Priya: depends on batch windowing; for interactive UX we use micro-batching with window under 20ms to keep p95 low; bigger batches help throughput but add tail. we can tune based on your p95 goals.
[00:06:15] Ethan: so we basically trade a few ms for big $ savings if we accept slightly longer tails?
[00:06:20] Priya: yep, and we can route high-priority low-latency requests to dedicated or hot pool, while routing cheaper background jobs to a lower-cost pool.
[00:06:30] Jordan: that's the routing policy idea — latency-first vs cost-first buckets.
[00:06:34] [00:07:00] Oliver: from procurement perspective we need a one-page pilot scope and expected spend. can you give ranges?
[00:07:07] Jordan: we'll provide low/medium/high spend bands for the pilot. example: pilot 2-week benchmark might cost $Y on hosted, or equivalent committed spend split across reserved capacity for dedicated.
[00:07:18] Oliver: and contract terms — do you allow short pilots without long-term lock?
[00:07:24] Jordan: yes pilots are zero-commit hosted or short-term reserved demos; a production committed dedicated is separate.
[00:07:31] Maya: what telemetry and observability will we get during pilot?
[00:07:35] Priya: token-level cost breakdown, per-route latency histograms, and trace hooks. we can push metrics to your prometheus/jaeger if you want.
[00:07:46] Ethan: great. for the benchmark we want to run: realistic traffic replay, 1-week run during peak/normal hours, measure p50/p95/p99, token cost, and quality regression on holdout eval prompts.
[00:07:58] Priya: sounds good. we'll need sample prompt sets and a traffic CSV.
[00:08:03] Ethan: i'll get that.
[00:08:06] [00:08:30] Jordan: let's talk numbers concrete — can you confirm monthly budget target?
[00:08:35] Ethan: we want predictability under $X/month for initial roll out; if costs are unpredictable we can't scale product.
[00:08:43] Jordan: understood. we'll model to that cap and show options to keep spend flat: batching, cache, model distillation/selection and routing.
[00:08:54] Maya: on the model side, do you host multiple model variants for fallback? e.g., a smaller low-cost model when latency spikes?
[00:08:59] Priya: yes, we can set canary/fallback policies — route to smaller model or lower precision when capacity constrained.
[00:09:08] Ethan: that could help smooth costs during spikes rather than paying for peak capacity.
[00:09:13] Jordan: exact point.
[00:09:16] [00:10:00] Maya: any dependencies on our side for dedicated? like VLANs, VPC peering?
[00:10:05] Priya: for dedicated you get network isolation; we need basic peering and permissions for metrics and health checks. for private on-prem it's deeper: install agent, KMS config.
[00:10:18] Oliver: procurement aside, timeline question — how fast can a pilot be standing?
[00:10:23] Jordan: we can start a hosted pilot within days, dedicated demo within 1-2 weeks depending on quota, private longer.
[00:10:31] Ethan: what about benchmarks in prod-like environment? we prefer dedicated-like environment for performance numbers.
[00:10:36] Priya: agreed — dedicated staging will reflect production latency/throughput more closely. we can spin a dedicated pool for the benchmark.
[00:10:44] Jordan: we'll size GPUs based on your token/sec; priya will propose hardware mix in the plan.
[00:10:51] [00:11:30] Ethan: quality testing — how do we guard against regression when we change quant or model?
[00:11:35] Priya: we'll run evals on fixed prompt sets with thresholds and set quality gates. optimize for cost while keeping those gates.
[00:11:43] Maya: ok, also data residency — all user content must stay in EU regions. is that possible?
[00:11:50] Jordan: yes, we have region controls and private deployments can be EU-only. dedicated can be provisioned in EU region as well. we'll note that as a constraint.
[00:11:59] Oliver: we'll need a statement of data residency for procurement.
[00:12:03] Jordan: will include in the security packet.
[00:12:07] [00:12:30] Ethan: let's talk about a real example — 1M tokens/day, 30% cache hit, expected monthly tokens ~30M. what's unit cost?
[00:12:40] Jordan: depends on model, but hypothetically hosted might be $A per 1k tokens; with 30% effective reduction and batching we show an effective $B per 1k. with dedicated reserved pricing that could drop further to $C per 1k assuming sustained usage. i'll put numbers in the workbook.
[00:12:58] Maya: do you include the KV cache memory overhead in the dedicated sizing?
[00:13:03] Priya: yes, cache sizing is part of capacity planning — more cache means more memory per replica.
[00:13:10] Ethan: what's the rollback strategy if a model/quantization causes quality issues mid-run?
[00:13:15] Priya: automatic fallback to previous model variant and automatic canary rollouts with metrics gating — we can revert traffic quickly.
[00:13:24] Jordan: also circuit-breakers for cost spikes — route to cheaper pool when cost thresholds hit.
[00:13:30] [00:14:00] Oliver: procurement question: any standard SLAs on latency?
[00:14:04] Jordan: enterprise SLA for dedicated can include latency SLOs; hosted has regional SLOs. we'll surface precise SLA terms in proposal.
[00:14:13] Maya: one more technical — does batching increase tokenization overhead or affect prompt ordering? sometimes batching reorders requests and that matters for session affinity.
[00:14:21] Priya: good point — we support session-aware batching and preserve ordering for session affinity; batching is mostly additive across independent requests.
[00:14:31] Ethan: ok that helps.
[00:14:35] [00:15:00] Jordan: next steps recap: jordan shares workbook; priya shares benchmark plan; verdant shares prompts and traffic; we schedule pilot week and procurement gets docs.
[00:15:12] Oliver: for procurement i'll need pilot cost estimate and PO template.
[00:15:17] Jordan: noted. will include.
[00:15:22] Ethan: one last question — if we start hosted pilot and later convert to dedicated, how hard is migration?
[00:15:28] Priya: it's primarily config and routing changes; same API surface, you can pin model versions. migration is usually straightforward — we help with rollout.
[00:15:38] Maya: excellent.
[00:15:42] [00:16:00] Priya: any blockers we haven't covered?
[00:16:04] Ethan: not yet. we'll confirm internal stakeholders for pilot next week.
[00:16:09] Oliver: procurement will start review once we get the one-pager.
[00:16:14] Jordan: great. i'll get the workbook out by friday (2026-04-09). priya will send benchmark plan by monday.
[00:16:23] Maya: thanks, appreciate the thoroughness.
[00:16:27] Ethan: thanks all.
[00:16:30] Jordan: okay we'll follow up with calendar invites for kickoff and a shared folder with docs, security packet, and the pricing xlsx (link placeholder: https://redwood.example/pricing/verdant-pilot).
[00:16:45] [00:17:00] -- End of main discussion; remaining minutes used for clarifying questions and sharing links --
[00:22:00] Priya: quick technical aside on caching math — if you average 30% cache hit on system prompts and 10% on user repeats, effective token reduction might be around 25% overall, but depends on prompt variance.
[00:27:00] Ethan: we should instrument early to measure cache hit real numbers, not just estimate.
[00:32:00] Jordan: agreed, pilot will include hit-rate instrumentation.
[00:37:00] Maya: procurement question — do you accept vendor questionnaires?
[00:37:08] Jordan: yes, send the form and we'll return within the week.
[00:42:00] Oliver: thanks everyone, that'll do it.

END TRANSCRIPT
